analogy.p: A stage magician makes the audience look at one hand while the other does the trick. The witches work like that: they draw Macbeth’s attention to the surface of their words (nobody can harm him, a wood cannot move) while the real meaning sits somewhere he does not look. The analogy shows why the prophecies seem trustworthy. It breaks down because the audience of a magic show consents to being fooled, while Macbeth is also fooling himself and is responsible for choosing to believe the comforting reading.

bullets: The theme appears at three levels: **people** (false faces), **perception** (hallucinations such as the dagger and the ghost) and **language** (the witches’ equivocating prophecies).
Its main function in the plot is to show the cost of deceit: Macbeth must lie to stay on the throne, and each lie isolates him further.
It also supports the tragic structure: the audience sees through the masks from the start (dramatic irony), so we watch Duncan trust the very man who plans to kill him.
The antithesis ‘fair/foul’ is reversed in meaning many times: a fair-seeming king’s guest is a murderer; a foul-seeming force (the witches) tells a partial truth.
The opposite of illusion is **truth and light**: the end of the play, with Malcolm’s ‘the time is free’, restores a world where words and reality match.

callouts.p: A statement that seems self-contradictory but contains a truth, such as ‘Fair is foul, and foul is fair’.
Treat ‘Fair is foul’ as the play’s thesis: the witches introduce a world of moral inversion, and Macbeth steps into it with his first line.

core.h: The central idea: a world where nothing is as it seems
core.p: The play opens with the witches chanting that ‘Fair is foul, and foul is fair’, and Macbeth’s first line, ‘So foul and fair a day I have not seen’, echoes them without his knowing. This **echo** is Shakespeare’s way of signalling that Macbeth has already entered the witches’ moral world, where good and evil are exchanged. From then on, almost every major character uses a disguise, sees an illusion or is fooled by a promise.

bullets: In Act 5 Scene 5 Macbeth himself names the problem: he begins to ‘doubt the equivocation of the fiend / That lies like truth’. Notice the paradox ‘lies like truth’, which is the same kind of structure as ‘Fair is foul’.
At 5.8 he accuses the witches of ‘juggling fiends’ that ‘palter with us in a double sense’. ‘Juggle’ suggests trickery and performance; ‘palter’ means to speak ambiguously.
Their language is full of **riddles and rhyming trochaic chants**, which sound like spells and make the prophecies feel authoritative, while their meaning stays slippery.
Macbeth’s mistake is deeply human: he interprets the prophecy in the way that suits him, which is a form of self-deception, not only the witches’ trick.

core.p: The witches do not lie outright. They use **equivocation**: language with a second meaning that makes the listener believe something false. Macbeth hears what he wants to hear, and the surface meaning blinds him to the possibility of another. The apparitions in Act 4 Scene 1 are the clearest example because each one gives him false confidence, and the Act 5 events turn the words against him.

head: Prophecy
How Macbeth reads it
What it really means
rows: ‘none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth’ (4.1)
No living man can hurt him
Macduff was ‘Untimely ripped’ from his mother (5.8), so he was not born in the normal way
He will not be vanquished until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane (4.1)
A forest cannot walk, so he is safe
Malcolm’s army cuts boughs as camouflage (5.4) and the wood appears to move
A warning he can handle, so he plans a pre-emptive attack
Macduff is his killer; the attack on Macduff’s family hardens Macduff’s vengeance
Banquo’s children will rule: a threat that must be removed
Banquo’s son Fleance escapes, so the prophecy remains alive
The first title arrives without effort, the second only through murder

bullets: Macbeth takes up the idea in 1.7: ‘False face must hide what the false heart doth know’. The repeated adjective makes the same word apply to both face and heart: both are false, so there is no honest part of him left. The closing rhyming couplet gives the line a sense of finality.

In Act 1 Scene 4 Duncan reflects that ‘There’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face’, and in the same breath welcomes Macbeth. The audience knows Macbeth has just hidden his ‘black and deep desires’, so Duncan’s trust is painfully ironic.

In Act 1 Scene 6 Duncan praises the castle’s ‘pleasant seat’, and Banquo notes the ‘temple-haunting martlet’ nesting there. These images of sweetness and sanctuary are dramatic irony, since the castle is about to be the site of a murder.

After the murder in Act 2 Scene 3, Macbeth performs grief and then kills the grooms, claiming rage. Donalbain’s line, ‘There’s daggers in men’s smiles’, is a metaphor of deceit that sums up the court in one sentence.

In Act 3 Scene 2 Macbeth tells his wife to ‘Make our faces vizards to our hearts, / Disguising what they are’. A vizard is a mask, so this is a theatrical image: they will perform as host and hostess.

callouts.p: Whenever a character trusts Macbeth (Duncan in 1.4 and 1.6, Banquo accepting the banquet invitation in 3.1), name it as dramatic irony and say what the audience knows that the character does not. This is where the tension and tragic pity come from.

core.h: False faces: the Macbeths and Duncan
core.p: Lady Macbeth’s advice in Act 1 Scene 5 is the clearest statement of the theme in action: ‘Look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under’t’. The instruction is to seem harmless while being deadly. The flower and serpent image also recalls the Garden of Eden, which a Jacobean audience would notice. In the same scene she tells him his face ‘is as a book where men / May read strange matters’, meaning his expression betrays his thoughts, so he must hide them.

bullets: The clothing image is also political: a rightful king wears a crown that fits. Macbeth’s robes do not fit because he is a usurper. This links appearance and reality to legitimacy.

There are theatre metaphors too. In Act 5 Scene 5 Macbeth calls life ‘a walking shadow, a poor player’. The self-aware reference to acting turns the whole play into a comment on performance, and a Jacobean audience in a theatre would hear that comment about themselves.

In the sleepwalking scene Lady Macbeth’s performance falls away: her private actions (washing hands, speaking of blood) show what her public face hid. Appearance and reality finally merge, and the truth emerges when she cannot control her mind.

Shakespeare uses costume and stage business: Duncan arrives in daylight, the murder happens at night, and Macbeth enters with bloody hands. The visual contrast between a clean appearance and a bloody reality is theatrical shorthand.

callouts.p: Clothing, masks, flowers hiding snakes and actors all show the same idea: outward show without matching inward truth.
Do not write ‘Shakespeare uses clothing imagery’ and stop. Say what it shows (Macbeth’s identity does not fit), where it shows it (1.3), and why it matters (he is a usurper).

core.p: Shakespeare repeatedly uses clothing as a metaphor for false identity. When Ross greets Macbeth as Thane of Cawdor, Macbeth asks, ‘why do you dress me / In borrowed robes?’ The title belongs to someone else, so Macbeth is wearing another man’s identity. The image recurs when Banquo says Macbeth’s new honours ‘cleave not to their mould’, just as new clothes do not fit until worn, and in Act 5 Angus says Macbeth’s title hangs loose ‘like a giant’s robe / Upon a dwarfish thief’, which makes the same point with an image of a robe that is too big.

bullets: The question ‘Is this a dagger which I see before me’ uses a long, searching sentence and rhetorical question. It dramatises indecision and, because it is addressed to an object, it shows how isolated he already is.
The dagger may be real (a supernatural guide), a hallucination caused by the ‘heat-oppressed brain’, or a projection of his conscience. Offering these options is useful for AO1.

In Act 3 Scene 4 the ghost of Banquo appears only to Macbeth. Lady Macbeth sees nothing and calls it ‘the very painting of your fear’. Here reality (an empty stool) clashes with Macbeth’s appearance (a terrified king), and the lords see the king break down.

Macbeth tells the ghost that it has ‘no speculation in those eyes’. ‘Speculation’ meant sight or the power of seeing, so he says the dead eyes cannot see, and the line shows he is the one who cannot see clearly.

The unreliability of perception connects to Banquo’s earlier question about the witches: ‘Were such things here’, asked of the weird sisters, and his talk of the ‘insane root’ that ‘takes the reason prisoner’. Even sensible Banquo doubts what he sees.

callouts.p: Use the dagger and ghost to bridge to the guilt theme: they are projections of conscience, so appearance and reality are tied to psychological truth.

core.h: Illusions of the mind: the dagger and the ghost
core.p: Macbeth’s perceptions are unstable once he has committed to murder. In Act 2 Scene 1 he sees a dagger that points towards Duncan’s chamber, and asks whether it is ‘a dagger of the mind, a false creation’. He cannot tell whether it is a vision from outside or his own conscience. Seconds later he says ‘Mine eyes are made the fools o’ the other senses’: his senses disagree, and he cannot trust the evidence of his sight.

bullets: In Act 2 Scene 4 Ross and the Old Man note that ‘dark night strangles the travelling lamp’ even though it is day by the clock. The verb ‘strangles’ is violent and personifies darkness as a murderer, while the ‘lamp’ is the sun: a nature-based version of appearance versus reality.

In Act 3 Scene 2 Macbeth says ‘Light thickens’ and describes the crow heading for the ‘rooky wood’: it is a night image in which light seems physically to become solid and dark, like a liquid thickening.

In Act 5 Scene 1 the doctor and gentlewoman note that Lady Macbeth keeps a light by her continually. Her fear of the dark shows that the concealment she used is unbearable for her, so the imagery reverses.
When Macbeth says ‘Out, out, brief candle’ at the news of his wife’s death, life is a brief flame that goes out, and he identifies his own world as dark.
At the end Malcolm and Macduff restore light: Macduff declares ‘the time is free’ (5.8), and the language of healing and daylight returns.

core.h: Light, dark and inverted day and night
core.p: Darkness is the setting of deception, and light is truth. In Act 1 Scene 4 Macbeth begs the stars to ‘hide your fires’ and not let light see his ‘black and deep desires’. He asks the cosmos itself to collude in his concealment. In Act 1 Scene 5 Lady Macbeth calls for ‘thick night’ and ‘the dunnest smoke of hell’, so that her knife will not ‘see the wound it makes’. The play’s many night scenes reflect hidden crime.

bullets: In Act 5 Scene 4 Malcolm orders every soldier to cut a bough from Birnam Wood so they ‘shadow / The numbers of our host’. Camouflage defeats a tyrant, and the fake wood becomes the instrument of fate, so appearance is also a tool of justice.
This complicates the theme: deception is not evil in itself. The distinction is purpose. The Macbeths deceive to commit regicide; Malcolm deceives to expose a spy and defeat a tyrant.
Malcolm’s reflection that ‘Angels are bright still, though the brightest fell’ acknowledges that good things can look bad and bad can look good: it makes the audience cautious about surfaces.
Duncan’s mistake (trusting by outward appearance) is the opposite error. Malcolm learns from it and tests before he trusts, which suggests wise kingship requires discernment.

callouts.p: Writing that all appearances in the play are deceptive is too simple. The ending shows that the legitimate side also uses disguise, which suggests the play is about **purpose and justice**, not only about honesty.

core.h: Deception used for good: Malcolm and the army
core.p: Not all disguise is evil, and a strong answer notices this. In Act 4 Scene 3 Malcolm tests Macduff by pretending to be lustful and greedy, claiming that ‘black Macbeth / Will seem as pure as snow’ beside him. He is acting, but for a loyal purpose: to see if Macduff is a spy. When Macduff reacts with despair, Malcolm drops the act and calls him ‘child of integrity’.

bullets: The Porter in Act 2 Scene 3 jokes about an ‘equivocator’ who could ‘swear in both the scales against either scale’. This is a clear reference to the contemporary debate over equivocation: the trial of the Jesuit Henry Garnet in 1606 brought the idea of misleading answers to the public’s attention.
King James believed in witchcraft and wrote Daemonologie (1597). Witches could create illusions in this belief system, so the witches’ power over appearances would have seemed real.
The theatre itself is a world of illusion and disguise: boy actors played women, and the language of ‘player’ and ‘shadow’ was self-aware for the Globe audience.
The Divine Right of Kings meant a king was God’s representative, so a false king (Macbeth) was a false image of the divine, a mask over illegitimate rule.
Use context sparingly and precisely: name the event, say where in the text it echoes, and explain the effect on the audience.

callouts.p: Using words that have more than one meaning in order to mislead the listener without technically lying.
‘For a Jacobean audience recently shaken by the Gunpowder Plot, Duncan’s trust in 1.4 would be especially unsettling because it dramatises how treachery hides behind a loyal face.’

core.h: Context for AO3: Jacobean fears of deceit
core.p: Macbeth was probably first performed around 1606, soon after the Gunpowder Plot of November 1605, in which Catholic conspirators hid barrels of gunpowder beneath the Houses of Parliament while apparently remaining loyal to the king. The discovery made treachery under a friendly face a national fear, and the play echoes it in Duncan’s trust and the Macbeths’ welcome.

bullets: When the extract is 1.5, 1.7 or 2.1: name the technique, quote a few words and say how it conceals or reveals something. Track the change from hidden thought to spoken action.
For part (b), choose moments from different parts of the play: prophecy (1.3), false faces (1.5/1.7), dagger (2.1), ghost (3.4), equivocation (5.8).
Strong thesis example: Shakespeare presents appearance and reality as a trap, in which those who perform false roles lose their grip on truth, while those who see clearly restore order.
Always ask: who is being deceived, who knows, and what does the audience feel?

callouts.p: A word, then the sentence structure, then the whole scene, then context. For example: ‘lies like truth’ is a simile inside a paradox, and it echoes the play’s opening line.
Do not write ‘Macbeth pretends to be nice’. Write precisely: who he deceives, what he hides, what words he uses, and what the effect is.

core.h: Exam technique for appearance and reality
core.p: This theme is easy to describe and hard to analyse. High marks come from showing how Shakespeare’s choices (antithesis, paradox, imagery, structure) embody the theme, and from explaining why the theme matters to the play’s moral message. Avoid simple lists of moments.

plan: Opening paradox and Macbeth’s echo of it as a signal of entering the witches’ world
Lady Macbeth’s flower and serpent advice and the cost of performance
Macbeth’s unstable perception: dagger and ghost
The prophecies’ equivocation and Macbeth’s self-deception
Counter-argument: Malcolm’s justified disguise and the restoration of light
essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents ideas about appearance and reality in Macbeth. Write about the extract from Act 1 Scene 5 and the play as a whole.
essays.text:
From the first scene, Shakespeare establishes a world in which categories are unstable. The witches’ paradox, ‘Fair is foul, and foul is fair’, uses the chiasmus of its structure to make moral values seem interchangeable, and when Macbeth enters with his first line, ‘So foul and fair a day I have not seen’, he echoes them without knowing it. This is a structural signal that he has already entered their moral world, before any prophecy has been spoken. The theme therefore operates from the opening, and the rest of the play dramatises what it costs to live in a reality where the surface is unreliable.

The cost is shown most clearly in Lady Macbeth’s instructions to her husband in Act 1 Scene 5. ‘Look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under’t’ is an imperative that treats character as a matter of costume. The contrast between a flower and a serpent echoes the Garden of Eden, so a Jacobean audience would recognise the connotations of temptation and a hidden threat to a paradise (here, Duncan’s court). She also tells him that his face is ‘a book’ that people can read, so what troubles her is not his thoughts but their visibility. Shakespeare gives deception a theatrical vocabulary, which Macbeth takes up in Act 3 when he asks that their faces be ‘vizards’, or masks, to their hearts. The shift from his early plea for the stars to ‘hide your fires’ to his deliberate management of a mask shows how habit hardens a hidden desire into a performance.

However, performance never fully controls reality. In Act 2 Scene 1, as he moves towards Duncan’s chamber, Macbeth sees a dagger and asks whether it is ‘a dagger of the mind’. The word ‘mind’ locates the vision inside his head, so the line can be read as a supernatural guide, a hallucination, or conscience made visible. Its interrogative form dramatises indecision and, because he addresses an empty space, hints at how isolated he already is. At the banquet the same instability returns: Banquo’s ghost sits at the table, but Lady Macbeth sees only ‘the very painting of your fear’. Reality, an empty stool, collides with appearance, a king terrified before his nobles, and for a Jacobean audience who believed the king’s body mirrored the health of the state, the public breakdown of a ruler is a political as well as a psychological disaster.

The most insidious deception, though, is the one Macbeth practises on himself. The witches do not lie; they equivocate. The apparitions in Act 4 promise that ‘none of woman born’ can harm him and that Birnam Wood must move, and he reads both in the way that suits his hopes. In Act 5 the truth emerges through unexpected means: Malcolm’s soldiers carry boughs as camouflage and Macduff was ‘Untimely ripped’ from his mother. By the time Macbeth recognises the ‘equivocation of the fiend / That lies like truth’, the paradox sounds like the play’s first line returning, closing the circle. Written soon after the Gunpowder Plot and the public debates around equivocation, the speech would also speak to an audience wary of language that conceals treason beneath loyalty.

Yet the play does not suggest that all disguise is evil. Malcolm’s test of Macduff in Act 4, in which he pretends to vices to see how Macduff responds, and the use of Birnam boughs show that appearance can be used for justice. The difference is purpose, and Shakespeare lets the audience judge. At the end, Macduff’s declaration that ‘the time is free’ restores a reality in which words and things correspond, so the final effect is not simply that the world is deceptive, but that tyranny corrupts language itself and that legitimate rule is honest rule.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents appearance and reality as a trap that destroys those who adopt false faces: the Macbeths’ deceit and Macbeth’s misreading of the witches isolate them from truth, until the final restoration of an honest world.
why: AO1: the thesis is conceptual (appearance and reality as a trap) and develops through five stages, ending with a counter-argument.
AO2: analyses specific words and techniques (chiasmus, imperative, ‘mind’, ‘vizards’, paradox) and comments on structure (the echo in 1.3, the circle back to 1.1).
AO3: context is integrated (Eden, Jacobean belief in the king’s body and the state, Gunpowder Plot, equivocation) and tied to precise textual moments.
Alternative interpretations of the dagger (supernatural, hallucination, conscience) show exploratory thinking.
AO4: controlled, varied sentences and a precise critical vocabulary; quotations are short and embedded.

model: Thesis: deception is presented as the means of ambition but also as its trap
Extract: flower and serpent metaphor, imperatives, the face as a book
Link: ‘False face must hide’ (1.7), ‘vizards’ (3.2)
Contrast: the honesty of Malcolm and Macduff at the end
Context: Gunpowder Plot and fear of hidden treason; Eden allusion
Evaluate: deception isolates the Macbeths and fails to protect them
exam.q: Starting with this extract (Act 1 Scene 5, Lady Macbeth’s ‘Look like the innocent flower’ speech), explain how far Shakespeare presents deception as necessary for ambition. Refer to the extract and the play as a whole. (40 marks)
exam.tip: Check the marks on your paper. For ‘how far’, argue both sides: it is necessary in the plot but unsuccessful as a moral strategy.

model: Apparitions with riddling language that sounds authoritative
‘none of woman born’ and Birnam Wood: equivocation
Macbeth’s over-confident interpretation
Dramatic irony: the audience may suspect the loophole
Link to ‘fair is foul’ and the paradox structure
Context: King James’s interest in witchcraft; equivocation debate
exam.q: How does Shakespeare present the witches’ prophecies in Act 4 Scene 1? (20 marks, part (a)-style)
exam.tip: Focus on how the language is built to mislead, not only on what is promised.

Disagree: some characters are what they seem (Banquo, Macduff, Lady Macduff)

exam.tip: Use located quotations and explain the effect, not just the image.

mistakes.r: Say they equivocate: each statement is technically true but misleading, and Macbeth’s interpretation is part of the problem.
Explain it as a paradox that blurs moral boundaries and links to the inversion of the natural order, then show Macbeth echoing it in 1.3.
mistakes.w: Writing ‘fair is foul means good is bad’ with no more detail.

mistakes.r: Choose three or four key moments and analyse language and effect in each; build an argument about the cost of deception.
mistakes.w: Listing every disguise in the play.

mistakes.r: Explore both readings (supernatural, hallucination, conscience) and say which is most convincing and why.
mistakes.w: Treating the dagger as definitely real or definitely imaginary.

mistakes.r: Use Malcolm’s test and the Birnam boughs to show that deceit can serve justice, so purpose matters.
mistakes.w: Forgetting that Malcolm also uses disguise.

mistakes.r: Tie the fear of hidden treason to specific moments such as Duncan’s trust or the Porter’s equivocator.
Use two to five exact words and explain individual word choices (for example ‘strangles’ in 2.4).

quotes.a: The witches’ chant is a paradox that reverses moral categories. The chiasmus (fair, foul, foul, fair) makes the line sound like a spell and the symmetry suggests an unstable world where values swap. It sets the central theme and invites the audience to doubt appearances throughout.
quotes.c: Jacobean belief that witches inverted the natural order.
quotes.q: Fair is foul, and foul is fair

quotes.a: Macbeth’s first line echoes the witches’ words, so he is already linked to them before he meets them. The adjectives are the same pair in a new order, suggesting his mind contains both fair and foul. It may also foreshadow the mixed prospect of reward and crime.
quotes.c: Shows how supernatural influence works before any prophecy.
quotes.q: So foul and fair a day

quotes.a: Macbeth’s question to Ross casts the title Thane of Cawdor as clothing that belongs to someone else. The metaphor foreshadows his kingship, which will also be borrowed, and hints at an identity that does not fit. It also associates power with performance.
quotes.c: Usurpation was a deep fear in Jacobean thought.

quotes.a: Duncan admits he cannot read hidden thoughts from a face, a line that is deeply ironic because he praises the very man who is about to betray him. The architectural image of ‘construction’ suggests minds are built and concealed. The audience’s knowledge creates tragic pity for Duncan.
quotes.c: Echoes anxiety about treason after the Gunpowder Plot.
quotes.q: no art / To find the mind’s construction

quotes.a: Lady Macbeth’s imperative tells Macbeth to look harmless while being the serpent beneath. The contrast between a beautiful flower and a poisonous snake links to the Garden of Eden and shows evil as a hidden threat. The repeated sound of ‘look’ and ‘be’ sets appearance against reality.
quotes.c: The serpent in Eden; a Jacobean audience would recognise it.

quotes.a: Macbeth ends the scene on a rhyming couplet that makes his decision final. The repetition of ‘false’ ties the face and the heart together so no honest part remains. The modal ‘must’ shows that concealment has become a duty and not just a choice.
quotes.c: Hypocrisy is the opposite of the Jacobean ideal of an honest king.

quotes.a: Macbeth questions whether the dagger is a ‘false creation’, so he recognises that his own mind may be deceiving him. The prepositional phrase ‘of the mind’ locates the vision internally and suggests guilt before the act. It also dramatises the breaking down of reality.
quotes.c: Witches and spirits could cause illusions in Jacobean belief.

quotes.a: Donalbain’s metaphor contrasts smiles with hidden weapons: friendliness conceals violence. His words are prophetic and justify his flight, and they apply to the whole court that has just welcomed Macbeth. The plural ‘daggers’ suggests multiple, widespread threats.
quotes.c: Reflects the fear of hidden traitors after 1605.

quotes.a: Macbeth uses the image of a mask to describe the pretence of friendliness at the banquet. Choosing ‘vizards’ makes the courtly world a theatre. The line shows that he now uses disguise deliberately, where in Act 1 he asked the stars to hide his desires.
quotes.c: The theatre was a world of masks and boy actors.

quotes.a: Macbeth recognises the witches’ equivocation with a paradox that mirrors the first scene. The simile ‘like truth’ suggests that falsehood can look identical to truth. His realisation comes too late and shows the cost of trusting appearances.
quotes.c: Equivocation was a topical issue in 1606.

quotes.a: Macbeth’s accusation shows how the prophecies work. ‘Palter’ means to speak in a way that is ambiguous or deceitful. ‘Double sense’ names exactly the device of equivocation, and the line brings the theme to its conclusion at the moment of his fall.
quotes.q: palter with us in a double sense

summary: Macbeth is built on the gap between how things look and how they are: from the witches’ riddling ‘Fair is foul’ to the Macbeths’ false faces, the dagger that is not there and the prophecies that deceive. You need to explain how Shakespeare creates this theme through language, imagery and structure, and link it to Jacobean fears of deceit and equivocation.

terms.d: Language with two meanings used to mislead, such as the witches’ prophecies.
A statement that appears contradictory yet expresses a truth, such as ‘Fair is foul’.
A direct contrast of ideas in balanced phrases, e.g. fair and foul.
When the audience knows something the characters do not, such as the plot against Duncan while he praises the castle.
Two contradictory terms placed together, such as ‘bitter-sweet’; ‘foul and fair’ in one phrase works in a similar way.
A recurring image or idea, such as clothing, darkness or blood, that develops a theme.
When nature mirrors human emotion or events, such as the dark day after Duncan’s murder.
A mask; used by Macbeth to describe the false faces he and his wife must wear.
A speech to oneself, revealing true thoughts; the dagger speech is an example.
